questions.question: What makes a function 'higher-order'?
options: It runs faster than other functions
It takes a function as an argument, returns a function, or both
It is defined using the `function` keyword instead of an arrow function
questions.explanation: Being higher-order is about treating functions as values — accepting or producing them — which is why map/filter/reduce all qualify.

questions.question: Which of these is a pure function?
options: function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
questions.explanation: `add` always returns the same output for the same inputs and has no observable side effects — the others mutate external state, return non-deterministic values, or perform I/O.

questions.question: Why are pure functions considered easier to test than impure ones?
options: They run faster in all cases
Their output depends only on their inputs, so there's no hidden external state to set up or tear down
They never need test cases at all
They cannot contain any conditional logic
questions.explanation: Since a pure function's behavior is fully determined by its arguments, a test just needs to supply inputs and check the output — no mocking of external state required.

questions.question: What does currying transform a multi-argument function into?
options: A function that ignores all but its first argument
A sequence of functions, each taking one argument, that can be partially applied to create specialized versions
A function with no arguments at all
questions.explanation: Currying breaks `f(a, b)` into `f(a)(b)`, letting you call it with one argument at a time and reuse the partially-applied result, like `multiply(2)` becoming a reusable `double` function.
